                                                    Abstract:
 The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission) prepared a draft environmental
 impact statement (EIS) for the CCL Stage 4 Project and CCPL Expansion Project (Project), proposed
 by Corpus Christi Liquefaction Stage IV, LLC, Corpus Christi Liquefaction, LLC, and Cheniere
 Corpus Christi Pipeline, L.P. (collectively, the Applicants) in the above-referenced dockets. The
 Applicants propose to expand the existing Corpus Christi Liquefied Terminal in San Patricio and
 Nueces Counties, Texas; construct and operate the Corpus Christi Pipeline, a new, 42-inch-diameter,
 25.8-mile-long natural gas pipeline in San Patricio, Texas, as well as construct the new Sinton 2
 Compressor Station, two new meter stations, and other appurtenant facilities in San Patricio County,
 Texas. The purpose of the Project is to expand the Applicants’ liquified natural gas production
 capabilities to deliver up to a total of 2.75 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas to the CCL Terminal.
 The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, U.S. Department of Transportation – Pipeline and Hazardous
 Materials Safety Administration, U.S. Coast Guard, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric
 Administration – National Marine Fisheries Service, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and the U.S.
 Department of Energy participated as cooperating agencies in the preparation of the draft EIS.
 Commission staff conclude that construction and operation of the proposed Project, with the mitigation
 measures recommended in the draft EIS, would result in some adverse environmental effects; however,
 effects would be reduced to less-than-significant levels.
 Comments on the draft Environmental Impact Statement are due to the Commission on or before 5:00
 pm Eastern Time on November 9, 2026.

TO THE INTERESTED PARTY:

       The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission)
have prepared a draft environmental impact statement (EIS) for the CCL Stage 4 Project
and CCPL Expansion Project (Project), proposed by Corpus Christi Liquefaction Stage IV,
LLC, Corpus Christi Liquefaction, LLC, and Cheniere Corpus Christi Pipeline, L.P.
(collectively, the Applicants). 1 The Applicants propose to expand the existing Corpus
Christi Liquefied Terminal (CCL Terminal) in San Patricio and Nueces Counties, Texas;
construct and operate the Corpus Christi Pipeline (proposed pipeline), a new,
42-inch-diameter, 25.8-mile-long natural gas pipeline in San Patricio, Texas, as well as
construct the new Sinton 2 Compressor Station, two new meter stations, and other
appurtenant facilities in San Patricio County, Texas. The purpose of the Project is to expand
the Applicants’ liquified natural gas (LNG) production capabilities to meet immediate and
future global demand for LNG.

       Any person wishing to comment on the draft EIS may do so. To ensure
consideration of your comments on the proposal in the final EIS, it is important that the
Commission receive your comments on or before 5:00 pm Eastern Time on November
9, 2026. Instructions for filing comments are provided on page 4.

        FERC is the lead federal agency for authorizing interstate natural gas transmission
facilities under the Natural Gas Act of 1938 (NGA) and the lead federal agency for
preparation of the draft EIS. The draft EIS assesses the potential environmental effects of
the construction and operation of the Project in accordance with the requirements of the
National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) 2 and the Commission’s implementing

 regulations. 3 The principal purposes of the draft EIS are to: identify and assess the
potential effects on the natural and human environment; describe and evaluate reasonable
alternatives; identify and recommend mitigation measures; and facilitate public
involvement in the environmental review process. The EIS concludes that approval of the
proposed project, with the mitigation measures recommended in the EIS, would have some
limited adverse environmental effects; however, with implementation of the mitigation
measures recommended in the EIS, most effects would be avoided, mitigated, or reduced
to less-than-significant levels. Visual effects of flaring could have a moderate and long-
term effect on nearby residences, but would not be significant.
        The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) Galveston District, U.S. Department
of Transportation – Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, U.S. Coast
Guard, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration – National Marine Fisheries
Service, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and the U.S. Department of Energy participated
as cooperating agencies in the preparation of the draft EIS. Cooperating agencies have
jurisdiction by law or special expertise with respect to resources potentially affected by the
proposal and participate in the NEPA analysis. The USACE would adopt and use the final
EIS to consider the issuance of an Individual Permit under Section 404 of the Clean Water
Act and Section 10 of the Rivers and Harbors Act. Although the cooperating agencies
provided input to the conclusions and recommendations presented in the draft EIS, the
agencies would present their own conclusions and recommendations in their respective
Records of Decision (where applicable) for the Project.

       The draft EIS addresses the potential environmental effects of the construction and
operation of the following Project facilities:

       • CCL Stage 4 Project
               •       Four new large-scale liquefaction trains (Trains 4-7) and appurtenant
                       facilities;
               •       Two full containment, aboveground 220,000-cubic-meter LNG
                       storage tanks;
               •       A new marine berth and appurtenant facilities; and
               •       One enclosed marine ground flare and three multi-point ground flares.
       • CCPL Expansion Project
               •       Approximately 25.8 miles of 42-inch-diameter pipeline loop
                       (proposed pipeline);

                      appurtenant facilities at the new Sinton 2 Compressor Station;
              •       A new meter station (Stage 4 Custody Meter Station) within the CCL
                      Terminal;
              •       A new meter station (Traverse Meter Station) adjacent to the Sinton 2
                      Compressor Station; and
              •       Three new mainline valves along the pipeline route.
        The Commission mailed a copy of the Notice of Availability of the draft EIS to
federal, state, and local government representatives and agencies; elected officials; Native
American tribes; environmental and public interest groups; potentially affected landowners
and other interested individuals and groups; and media outlets and libraries in the project
area. The draft EIS is only available in electronic format. It may be viewed and
downloaded at (www.ferc.gov), on the natural gas environmental documents page
(https://www.ferc.gov/industries-data/natural-gas/environment/environmental-
documents). In addition, the draft EIS may be accessed by using the eLibrary link on
FERC’s website. Click on the eLibrary link (https://elibrary.ferc.gov/eLibrary/search),
select “General Search,” and enter the docket number in the “Docket Number” field,
excluding the last three digits (i.e. CP26-82, CP26-87, and CP18-513). Be sure you have
selected an appropriate date range. For assistance, please contact FERC Online Support at
FercOnlineSupport@ferc.gov or toll free at (866) 208-3676, or for TTY, contact (202) 502-
8659.

        The draft EIS is not a decision document. It presents Commission staff’s
independent analysis of the environmental issues for the Commission to consider when
addressing the merits of all issues in this proceeding. Under Section 3 of the NGA, the
FERC considers, as part of its decision to authorize natural gas facilities, all factors bearing
on the public interest. Specifically, regarding whether to authorize natural gas facilities
used for importation or exportation, the FERC shall authorize the proposal unless it finds
that the proposed facilities will not be consistent with the public interest. Under Section
7(c) of the NGA, the Commission determines whether interstate natural gas transportation
facilities are in the public convenience and necessity and, if so, grants a Certificate of
Public Convenience and Necessity to construct and operate them. Under Section 3 of the
NGA, regarding whether to authorize natural gas facilities used for importation or
exportation, the Commission shall authorize the proposal unless it finds that the proposed
facilities will not be consistent with the public interest.
      Your comments should focus on draft EIS’s disclosure and discussion of potential
environmental effects, measures to avoid or lessen environmental effects, and the
completeness of the submitted alternatives, information and analyses. For your
convenience, there are four methods you can use to submit your comments to the
Commission. The Commission encourages electronic filing of comments and has staff

 available to assist you at (866) 208-3676 or FercOnlineSupport@ferc.gov. Please carefully
follow these instructions so that your comments are properly recorded.
      1)     You can file your comments electronically using the eComment feature on
             the Commission’s website (www.ferc.gov) under the link to Documents and
             Filings. This is an easy method for submitting brief, text-only comments on
             a project.
      2)     You can file your comments electronically by using the eFiling feature on the
             Commission’s website (www.ferc.gov) under the link to Documents and
             Filings. With eFiling, you can provide comments in a variety of formats by
             attaching them as a file with your submission. New eFiling users must first
             create an account by clicking on “eRegister.” If you are filing a comment on
             a particular project, please select “Comment on a Filing” as the filing type.

      3)     You can file a paper copy of your comments by mailing them to the following
             address. Be sure to reference the Project docket numbers (i.e. CP26-82-000,
             CP26-87-000, and CP18-513-000) with your submission: Submissions sent
             via the U.S. Postal Service must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese,
             Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 888 First Street NE,
             Room 1A, Washington, DC 20426. Submissions sent via any other carrier
             must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy
             Regulatory Commission, 12225 Wilkins Avenue, Rockville, Maryland
             20852.

      4)     In lieu of sending written or electronic comments, the Commission invites
             you to attend the public comment session its staff will conduct in the Project
             area to receive comments on the draft EIS, scheduled as follows:

             The primary goal of this comment session is to have you identify the specific
             environmental issues and concerns with the draft EIS. Individual oral
             comments will be taken on a one-on-one basis with a court reporter. This
             format is designed to receive the maximum amount of oral comments in a
             convenient way during the timeframe allotted.
             The comment session is scheduled from 5:00 pm to 8:00 pm local time. You
             may arrive at any time after 5:00 pm. There will not be a formal presentation

                                           -4-
               by Commission staff when the session opens. If you wish to speak, the
              Commission staff will hand out numbers in the order of your arrival.
              Comments will be taken until 8:00 pm. However, if no additional numbers
              have been handed out and all individuals who wish to provide comments
              have had an opportunity to do so, staff may conclude the session at 7:30 pm.

              Your oral comments will be recorded by the court reporter (with FERC staff
              or representative present) and become part of the public record for this
              proceeding. Transcripts will be publicly available on FERC’s eLibrary
              system (see below for instructions on using eLibrary). If a significant
              number of people are interested in providing oral comments in the one-on-
              one settings, a time limit of 5 minutes may be implemented for each
              commentor. Although there will not be a formal presentation, Commission
              staff will be available throughout the comment session to answer your
              questions about the environmental review process.

              It is important to note that the Commission provides equal consideration
              to all comments received, whether filed in written form or provided
              orally at a comment session.

        Any person seeking to become a party to the proceeding must file a motion to
intervene pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedures
(18 CFR Part 385.214).         Motions to intervene are more fully described at
http://www.ferc.gov/resources/guides/how-to/intervene.asp. Only intervenors have the
right to seek rehearing or judicial review of the Commission’s decision. Simply filing
environmental comments will not give you intervenor status, but you do not need
intervenor status to have your comments considered.

Questions?
       For public inquiries and assistance with making filings such as interventions,
comments, or requests for rehearing, contact the Office of Public Participation at (202) 502-
6595 or OPP@ferc.gov. Additional information about the project is available from the
FERC website (www.ferc.gov) using the eLibrary link. The eLibrary link also provides
access to the texts of all formal documents issued by the Commission, such as orders,
notices, and rulemakings.

      In addition, the Commission offers a free service called eSubscription that allows
you to keep track of all formal issuances and submittals in specific dockets. This can
reduce the amount of time you spend researching proceedings by automatically providing
you with notification of these filings, document summaries, and direct links to the
documents.      Go to www.ferc.gov/docs-filing/esubscription.asp to register for
eSubscription.

        I certify that Commission staff has considered the factors mandated by the National
Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and that this environmental document represents a good-faith
effort to disclose the most important considerations required by NEPA within the statutory page
limit (42 U.S.C. § 4336a(e)) and the statutory deadline (42 U.S.C. § 4336a(g)). This certification
reflects staff’s expert judgment that the analysis contained within this environmental document is
an accurate representation of the potential environmental effects of the proposed action and the
analysis is substantially complete. In staff’s judgment, any considerations addressed briefly or left
unaddressed would not meaningfully inform the assessment of environmental effects.

        The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) has
prepared this draft Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) to fulfill the requirements of the
National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) 1 and the Commission’s implementing

Liquefaction, LLC (together CCL Stage IV) and Cheniere Corpus Christi Pipeline, L.P. (CCPL),
collectively (the Applicants), entered into FERC’s Pre-Filing Process. On February 3, 2026, CCL
Stage IV and CCPL filed a formal application with FERC under Sections 3 and 7(c) of the Natural
Gas Act (NGA) and parts 157 and 380 of the Commission’s regulations requesting authorization
to site, construct, and operate an expansion of the existing and approved liquefied natural gas
(LNG) terminal in San Patricio and Nueces Counties, Texas on the La Quinta Ship Channel (CCL
Terminal) 2 and site, construct, and operate interstate natural gas pipeline and ancillary facilities in
San Patricio County, Texas. Additionally, CCPL is requesting a limited amendment to its Stage 3
Pipeline Project, that was approved in Docket No. CP18-513-000, 3 to vacate part of the certificated
capacity because CCPL no longer intends to construct the approved 21 miles of 42-inch-diameter
Stage 3 Loop pipeline. The joint application was assigned Docket Nos. CP26-82-000, CP26-
87-000, and CP18-513-000. The purpose of the Project is to expand the Applicants’ LNG
production capabilities to meet immediate and future global demand for LNG. The CCPL
Expansion Project would deliver up to a total of 2.75 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of natural
gas to the existing CCL Terminal and the new CCL Terminal facilities would provide additional
liquefaction capacity of approximately 1,200 billion cubic feet per year (Bcf/y).

Surface Waters

        Two waterbodies were identified within the CCL Stage 4 Project: a minor ephemeral man-
made storm water feature and Corpus Christi Bay. CCL Stage IV would amend the existing
individual stormwater permit from the Texas Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (TPDES)
prior to placing Project facilities into service. CCL Stage IV would develop and implement a
stormwater pollution prevention plan that would include set practices to manage stormwater and
eliminate or minimize stormwater effects from its industrial activities. Corpus Christi Bay would
be affected by construction and operation of a third marine shipping berth and offloading facilities
at the CCL Terminal facilities. Effects include turbidity, sedimentation, and habitat loss from
dredging activities; noise and vibration effects from pile driving; rip rap installation for shoreline
protection; and barge and ship traffic which can cause temporary turbidity and wake waves that
can cause shoreline erosion. The Applicant would use appropriate dredging equipment, and if
needed, turbidity curtains, to minimize dredging effects. The Applicant would mitigate permanent
dredging effects on seagrass and wetland habitat through compensatory mitigation. Additional
ship traffic could result in increased shoreline erosion.

        The CCPL Expansion Project crosses seven intermediate waterbodies, including Oliver
Creek and Chiltipin Creek. CCPL would install the pipeline under three waterbodies, Oliver
Creek, Chiltipin Creek, and an excavated drainage ditch, via horizontal direction drill (HDD)
trenchless construction methods, thereby avoiding direct effects resulting from traditional pipeline
installation techniques. CCPL would cross two excavated drainage ditches via the open cut trench
method and two waterbodies using a temporary access road, and CCPL would avoid and/or
minimize effects on these ditches by implementing the Plan and Procedures, its Spill Prevention,
Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) Plan, and requirements of applicable federal and state
permits. We conclude that the Project, incorporating these mitigation measures, would not result
in significant long-term or permanent effects on surface water resources in the Project area.

Fisheries and Aquatic Resources

         Fisheries near the Project area are estuarine, marine, and freshwater fisheries. Construction
and operation of the new CCL Terminal Marine Facilities would temporarily affect 34.9 acres of
marine fish habitat, including Essential Fish Habitat (EFH), and permanently affect 8.4 acres of
marine habitat and EFH. We expect post-construction conditions would remain suitable for
supporting marine and estuarine species, and shallow-water-dependent life stage needs would be
met by other nearby shallow water habitats within Corpus Christi Bay unaffected by the Project.
CCL Stage IV proposes to offset these effects at a 3:1 mitigation ratio. With this draft EIS, we are
initiating our consultation with NOAA-NMFS regarding EFH effects.

would increase the potential for aquatic species vessel strikes. All vessels controlled or contracted
by CCL Stage IV would be required to adhere to the NOAA-NMFS Southeast Regional Office’s
(SERO) Vessel Strike Avoidance Measures and NOAA-NMFS SERO’s Protected Species
Construction Conditions. The measures include, but are not limited to, maintaining watch for
protected species, maintaining a buffer zone if protected species are sighted, reducing engine
speed, and reporting collisions or sightings of injured or dead species protected under federal law.
Additionally, CCL Stage IV would provide educational training for personnel involved in marine

sources include heavy construction machinery, marine vessels, and pile driving. With the
exception of pile driving, CCL Stage IV proposes to conduct general construction activities 24
hours per day for the duration of construction and conduct noise surveys in response to
substantiated noise complaints to verify compliance with applicable noise criteria and to evaluate
whether additional noise mitigation measures are necessary. Noise effects due to construction of
the CCPL Expansion Project are expected to have a minimal effect at any one location due to the
nature of pipeline construction continuously moving down the pipeline right-of-way. CCPL would
primarily limit construction of the pipeline and aboveground facilities to daytime hours; however,
discrete activities, including hydrostatic testing and radiographic testing, may require activity 24
hours per day. HDD activities would occur 24 hours a day; however, CCPL would implement
noise mitigation measures to reduce sound levels to below 55 dBA Ldn at NSAs. We recommend
that any Commission authorization require CCPL to monitor noise levels during nighttime
construction activities, including but not limited to HDD 3 installation; document the noise levels
in the biweekly status reports; and restrict the noise attributable to nighttime construction or
drilling operations to no more than 55 dBA Ldn (48.6 dBA Leq) at any nearby NSAs. Based on the
mitigation measures proposed, we conclude that construction noise effects would be temporary
and less than significant.

would remain below the 55 dBA Ldn threshold at all NSAs. To ensure sound levels are in
compliance with our noise requirements, we recommend that any Commission authorization for
the Project require the Applicants to provide the Commission with operational noise surveys after

Alternatives
        We considered and evaluated alternatives to the proposed Project, including the no-action
alternative, system alternatives, major route and aboveground facility alternatives, minor route
variations, and offsite construction yard alternatives. The no-action alternative would avoid the
environmental effects associated with construction and operation of the proposed Project;
however, the Applicants would not be able to expand their LNG production capabilities to meet
immediate and future global demand for LNG. We have prepared this EIS to inform the
Commission and stakeholders about the expected effects that would occur if the Project were
constructed and operated. The Commission would ultimately determine the Project need and could
choose the no-action alternative.

        We evaluated potential system alternatives for the two pipelines currently supplying natural
gas to the CCL Terminal, along with other intrastate gas pipelines in the Project area and concluded
that none have sufficient capacity to meet the proposed export volume without additional pipeline
infrastructure. We evaluated multiple alternative sites for the CCL Stage 4 and the CCPL
Expansion Aboveground facilities. Upon review of environmental and technical factors, we
concluded that the alternative site options do not provide significant environmental advantages
over the proposed sites. We evaluated two major pipeline route alternatives and neither offered
significant environmental advantages over the proposed route. Two minor route variations were
identified by a landowner and neither offered significant environmental advantages over the
proposed route. For the reasons discussed above, we conclude that the proposed Project, with our
recommended mitigation measures, is the preferred alternative to meet the Project objective.

Conclusions
        For most resources, the construction and operation of the Project would result in limited
adverse environmental effects. Most adverse environmental effects would be temporary or short-
term during construction, but some long-term and permanent environmental effects would occur
on wetlands, seagrass areas, visual resources, and air quality. Visual effects of flaring could have
moderate and long-term effects on nearby residences, but would not be significant. This
determination is based on our review of the information provided by the Applicants and further
developed from environmental information requests; scoping; literature research; consideration of
potential alternatives; contacts with federal, state, and local agencies; and other stakeholders. We
conclude that effects would be less than significant with implementation of the Applicants’
proposed avoidance, minimization, and mitigation measures as well as the environmental
conditions we recommend the Commission include in any Project authorization it may issue.

four liquefaction trains, two LNG storage tanks, three ground flares, a third marine berth, a
terminal supply line, and other associated infrastructure. Once completed, expansion of the CCL
Terminal and operation of the proposed pipeline would increase the number of LNGC exports from
the terminal from approximately 480 per year to 870 per year. The expanded facilities would be
sited on property owned by an affiliate of Cheniere Energy, Inc. All components would be sited,
constructed, owned, operated, and maintained in accordance with applicable federal and state

sulfide, heavy hydrocarbons, water, and mercury from the feed gas; waste heat recovery systems
for regenerating the gas driers and amine system; induced draft air coolers; associated fire and gas
and safety systems; associated control systems and electrical infrastructure; utility connections and
distribution systems; and piping, piperacks, foundations, and structures within the LNG train
battery limits. Six low emission gas turbine-driven refrigerant compressors would operate when

toluene, ethylbenzene, xylene, and acid gas would be removed from the natural gas stream prior

construction. However, a 10-foot-wide vegetation strip may be hand cleared between the HDD
entry and exit points to facilitate placement of HDD guide wires and monitoring for inadvertent

additional guide wires necessary to generate electromagnetic fields to guide the drill during the
HDD process. To complete each HDD, a drill rig is placed on the crossing’s entry side, and a
borehole is drilled along a predetermined path beneath the feature. Throughout the drilling
process, a fluid mixture consisting primarily of water and bentonite clay (a naturally occurring
mineral) is pumped into the drill hole to lubricate the drill bit as it cuts through the subsurface
material, transport cuttings to the surface, and maintain the integrity of the hole. HDD drill cuttings
would not be disposed of in environmentally sensitive areas such as wetlands, waterbodies, or
sensitive species habitats. Once the borehole is completed, the assembled pipeline is pulled from
the exit side back through the borehole.

         We evaluated potential alternatives to the Project to determine whether an alternative would
be environmentally preferable, reasonable, and/or technically and economically feasible to the
proposed Project. We considered or evaluated alternatives including the no-action alternative,
system and design alternatives, major route alternatives, minor route variations, and aboveground

         We compared each alternative to the proposed Project using the following three evaluation
criteria:
       1.      ability of the alternative to meet the Project’s objectives;
       2.      reasonableness, practicality, and technical feasibility of the alternative; and
       3.      consideration of whether the alternative would have a significant environmental
               advantage over the proposed Project.
        For the purposes of NEPA, and in association with the first criterion above, the main
objective of the Project is to expand the Applicants’ LNG production capabilities to meet
immediate and future global demand for LNG. The Applicants have proposed expansion of the
existing CCL Terminal and additional gas transmission capacity into the CCL Terminal to meet
this objective.

3.1    ALTERNATIVE EVALUATION PROCESS

        Alternatives that would not meet the Project’s objective or would not be feasible were not
brought forward to the next level of review (i.e., the third evaluation criterion). Some alternatives
may be limited by the extent of system capacities, while others may not be practical because sites
are unavailable or cannot be developed for the proposed use. Our evaluation of the identified
alternatives is based on Project-specific information provided by the Applicants, stakeholder
comments, publicly available information, and our expertise and experience regarding the siting,
construction, and operation of natural gas transmission facilities and their potential effects on the
environment.

3.2    NO-ACTION ALTERNATIVE

        If the Commission selects the no-action alternative, then the Project facilities would not be
constructed, the potential effects from the proposed Project would not occur, and the Project’s
objective would not be met. The no-action alternative would avoid the environmental effects
associated with construction and operation of the proposed Project; however, CCPL would not be
able to provide additional natural gas to the CCL Terminal and CCL Stage IV would not increase
its export capacity from the CCL Terminal.

       We have not identified any reasonably foreseeable environmental consequences of not
implementing the proposed action; it is speculative to determine what other actions may be
proposed to support worldwide natural gas needs. We have prepared this EIS to inform the
Commission and stakeholders about the expected effects that would occur if the Project were to

3.3    PIPELINE SYSTEM ALTERNATIVES

        System alternatives are alternatives to a proposed project that would meet the project
objectives but would utilize a different (often existing) natural gas facility and/or pipeline system,
or a different configuration of facilities, which would eliminate the need to construct all or part of
the proposed project. The purpose of identifying and evaluating system alternatives is to determine
whether potential environmental effects associated with the construction and operation of the
proposed facilities could be avoided or reduced while still meeting the Project’s basic objectives.
Accordingly, we can attempt to identify (to the extent possible) other LNG export terminals and/or
other existing natural gas pipeline systems that could meet the objective of exporting natural gas
to the world market. However, it is outside of the scope of this EIS to direct other companies to
design or construct a project that would take the place of the proposed Project. Additionally, the
purpose of the Project is to increase natural gas export from the existing CCL Terminal. Evaluating
other LNG terminals would not meet the purpose of the Project. Therefore, we are focusing our
analysis of system alternatives on those that the Applicants could implement at the CCL Terminal
or adjacent lands.

        A viable system alternative to the proposed CCPL Expansion Project would require an
equivalent volume of natural gas to be transported to the CCL Terminal through modifications or
expansions of other natural gas pipelines. Additionally, the system alternative must be technically
and economically practical and offer a significant environmental advantage over the proposed
Project. Our analysis of system alternatives includes an examination of existing and proposed
natural gas transportation systems that could provide a similar delivery capacity as the proposed
CCPL Expansion Project.

        Two pipelines currently transport natural gas to the CCL Terminal, CCPL’s existing
pipeline and the Agua Dulce-Corpus Christi pipeline. Based on current design and operation
capacity of these pipelines, there is insufficient available capacity to meet the equivalent volume
needs of the proposed Project. Other local pipeline systems, including the Kinder Morgan Tejas
Ingleside lateral, EPO South Texas TX150 line, Energy Transfer Gregory Line, KM
Tejas/Southcross line, and the Boardwalk Intrastate Mustang Island Line, currently supply the
municipalities of Sinton, Taft, Gregory, Portland, Ingleside, and Aransas Pass, Texas, as well as
industrial facilities and power plants in the general vicinity of the CCL Terminal. While specific
information on sizes and capacities of these intrastate pipelines is not public information, these
lines are generally less than 20 inches in diameter and have total capacities between 50 million
and 200 million standard cubic feet per day. Similarly, these pipelines or a combination of these
pipelines could not provide the equivalent volume needs of the proposed Project. Therefore,
additional pipeline infrastructure would be required to meet the volume needs of the Project.
Construction of new pipeline infrastructure and associated aboveground facilities (e.g.,
compression facilities, meter stations, and MLVs) would likely result in environmental effects that
would be similar to the proposed Project. Given that none of these existing systems would meet
the Project objectives, and that we cannot direct other companies to design or construct projects to
take the place of the proposed Project, system alternatives were not further considered.

4.1    ENVIRONMENTAL TRENDS AND PLANNED ACTIVITIES

       To characterize the environmental baseline and contextualize the Project’s effects, we
describe the existing environment in the Project area, how the environment has changed over time,
and other reasonably foreseeable projects in the area.

        San Patricio and Nueces Counties are along the Texas Coastal Bend and share a subtropical
coastal climate characterized by hot summers, mild winters, and variable precipitation with
periodic drought and tropical storm influences (NOAA-NCDC, 2026). The region lies within the
Gulf Coastal Plain, with relatively flat to gently sloping terrain shaped by alluvial and marine
depositional processes. Underlying geology consists primarily of unconsolidated sediments,
including sands, silts, and clays (Brown et al., 1976). These conditions contribute to poorly drained
soil in some low-lying areas and support extensive estuarine systems associated with Corpus
Christi Bay and the Nueces River.

        San Patricio County was formed in 1836 and has experienced steady population growth
driven by industrial development and proximity to the Corpus Christi metropolitan area, with
current estimates nearing 70,000 residents. Nueces County, established in 1846, has a larger
population exceeding 350,000, centered around the City of Corpus Christi. Population growth in
both counties accelerated during the 20th and early 21st centuries due to expansion of the
petrochemical, refining, port, and logistics industries. Land use in the region has transitioned from
predominantly agricultural and ranching operations to a mixed landscape of industrial facilities,
transportation corridors, urban development, and remaining agricultural lands. San Patricio
County continues to support agriculture, including row crops, cattle grazing, and hay production,
while Nueces County is more urbanized, with economic activity focused on port operations, energy
infrastructure, manufacturing, and tourism (Texas State Historical Association, 2026).

      Both counties are within coastal watershed systems that drain into the Nueces River and
Corpus Christi Bay (USGS, 2025a). These systems are influenced by both natural hydrologic

 variability and anthropogenic inputs, including nutrients, sediment, and industrial discharges.
Surface water quality may be affected by agricultural runoff, urban stormwater, and industrial
activities, particularly in developed areas near the Port of Corpus Christi. Air quality in the Project
area is in attainment for all federal air quality standards. However, transboundary pollution events
can temporarily degrade air quality and influence ambient conditions.

        Recent land cover trends in the Project area reflect continued industrial expansion,
particularly in San Patricio County, where large-scale energy and petrochemical developments
have resulted in conversion of agricultural lands and open space to industrial use. Additional
changes include expansion of transportation infrastructure, port facilities, and associated utility
corridors. Planned and ongoing developments in the vicinity of the CCL Stage 4 Project include
pipeline infrastructure, electrical transmission facilities, roadway improvements, and commercial
and residential development projects. 45 These activities may contribute to incremental changes in
the environmental baseline through temporary construction-related effects such as vegetation
clearing, soil disturbance, and air emissions from construction equipment, as well as long-term

4.2.2   HDD Feasibility

        The HDD pipeline construction methods are described in section 2.6.4.1. The length of an
HDD, the pipe diameter, and the subsurface conditions are factors that determine the technical
feasibility of installation. Subsurface conditions that can affect feasibility of an HDD include
excessive rock strength and abrasiveness, unconsolidated gravel and boulder materials, poor
bedrock quality, solution cavities, and artesian conditions. It is also possible for HDD pipeline
installations to fail, primarily due to encountering unexpected geologic conditions such as
transitioning from coarse unconsolidated materials into bedrock or if the pipe were to become
lodged in the hole during pullback.

         During HDD activities, drilling fluid consisting primarily of water and bentonite clay is
pumped under pressure through the inside of the drill pipe and flows back (returns) to the drill
entry point along an annular space between the outside of the drill pipe and the drilled hole. In
certain conditions the drilling fluid can seep into the surrounding rocks and sediment. Drilling
fluid losses typically occur when the drilling fluid flows through the porous spaces in the soil
through which the HDD profile passes or within fractures contained in the rock formation.
Inadvertent releases of drilling fluid are more likely to occur in more permeable soils or via
fractures or fissures in bedrock. The risk of an inadvertent release occurring is greatest near the
drill entry and exit points, where the drill path has the least amount of ground cover.

        The Applicants propose the HDD method to cross infrastructure (e.g., roads, railroads, and
utility corridors) and sensitive resources (e.g., wetlands and waterbodies) at six locations as
presented in table 2.5.4-1. Geotechnical investigations have been completed for each of the HDD
crossings 46 and no geotechnical issues are present.

4.2.5   Geologic Hazards

        Geologic hazards are natural, physical conditions that can result in damage to land and
structures or injury to people. Such hazards are often seismic-related, including earthquakes,
surface faulting, and soil liquefaction. The following sections include a discussion of seismic
hazards, landslides, ground subsidence (including karst terrain), corrosion, and flood hazards.

4.2.5.1 Seismicity and Soil Liquefaction

        Seismic hazards include earthquakes, ground faulting, and secondary effects such as soil
liquefaction. Earthquake severity can be expressed in terms of intensity and magnitude. Intensity
is based on observed effects of ground shaking, while magnitude describes seismic energy released
at the earthquake source. The USGS publishes probabilistic seismic hazard analyses for the United
States under their Hazard Mapping Program, the goal of which is to quantify the rate (or
probability) of exceeding various ground motion levels at a given location. Project components
are in areas with a less than 1 percent chance of minor-damage ground shaking from an earthquake
(USGS, 2026b).

        Class B normal faults (USGS, 2026c) are located across the Gulf Coast (USGS, 2026d)
and are described as faults that show evidence of the existence of a fault or suggest Quaternary
deformation, but either the fault might not extend deeply enough to be a potential source of
significant earthquakes, or the currently available geologic evidence is too strong to confidently
assign the feature to a lower class but not strong enough to assign it to a higher class. The gulf-
margin normal faults exist in sediments and poorly lithified rocks. Most of these materials may
be unable to support the stresses required for the propagation of significant seismic ruptures that
could cause damaging ground motions (Crone and Wheeler, 2000).

      Soil liquefaction may occur when loose, cohesionless, and water-saturated soils are
exposed to ground shaking due to an earthquake. Based on the low seismic hazard, this risk is
low. As a result, we do not expect liquefaction to significantly affect the Project.

4.3.1.3 Soil Compaction
        Soil compaction occurs when the pore space between soil particles is reduced because of
soil particles being pressed together, thus changing the soil’s strength and drainage properties and
reducing its water-retention capacity. As a result, soil productivity and plant growth rates may be


                                                4-8
 diminished, soils may have a greater erosion potential, and natural drainage patterns may be
modified, which is of particular concern in agricultural and hydric soils. The susceptibility of soils
to compaction varies based on moisture content, composition, grain size, and density of the soil.
Project construction could result in loss of soil productivity due to compaction, or other damage
to soil structure from heavy equipment. Soil structural damage and compaction could also result
from pipeline construction during excessively wet periods. To minimize potential effects on soil
compaction, the Applicants would implement the measures contained in the Plan and Procedures,
which include but are not limited to testing topsoil and subsoil for compaction at regular intervals,
decompacting subsoil before replacing segregated topsoil, and conducting additional tilling as
needed where construction or cleanup activities have resulted in further compaction. In areas with
wet or poorly drained soils, the Applicants would further reduce compaction by restricting work
during unsuitable weather conditions, utilizing low ground pressure or wide-track equipment and
using construction mats as needed.

4.3.1.4 Low Revegetation Potential
        Soils that have low revegetation potential are considered areas of revegetation concern.
The vegetation potential of soils is based on several characteristics, including topsoil thickness,
soil texture, available water capacity, susceptibility to flooding, and slope, but also considers
whether the soils are natural, human transported, disturbed, or at high risk for seed mortality. Soils
with poor revegetation potential may need additional management and may be difficult to
revegetate, which can lead to increased erosion, reduction in wildlife habitat, and adverse visual
effects. The land capability classification is a system of grouping soils primarily based on
capability to produce common cultivated crops and pasture plants without deteriorating over a long
period of time (NRCS, 2026b).

        The Applicants would promote revegetation through the implementation of measures from
the Plan and Procedures, including but not limited selecting and applying appropriate seed mixes
and fertilizer as recommended; seeding permanent vegetation within recommended seeding dates;
preparing the seedbed in disturbed areas up to 3 to 4 inches deep using appropriate equipment;
implementing temporary stabilization measures (e.g., using mulch in upland areas); and follow-up
monitoring after the first growing season, and if necessary, the second growing season to determine
success of revegetation. The Applicants would promote revegetation of upland soils disturbed by
the Project using seed mixes based on recommendations approved and specified by local soil
conservationists and/or land management agencies or landowner agreements. The restoration of
affected lands is a process and may be accomplished relatively quickly (1 to 2 growing seasons)
or may require several years to complete, depending on several factors. Restoration of affected
lands can be adversely affected by weather conditions such as drought or abnormal rainfall,
landowner actions (e.g., physical changes to land use, cattle grazing), and/or third-party actions
including non-Project use/activities. If initial restoration activities are unsuccessful, the
Applicants, in consultation with the affected landowner and consistent with our environmental
compliance monitoring and reporting requirements, would continue to assess, take action, and
implement measures to ensure the eventual restoration of the affected resources.

other routine maintenance dredging within the La Quinta Ship Channel. We expect post-
construction conditions would remain suitable for supporting marine and estuarine species, and
shallow-water-dependent life stage needs would be met by other nearby shallow water habitats
within Corpus Christi Bay that would not be affected by the Project. Therefore, dredging and
filling activities would have moderate, but not significant effects on fisheries.

installation would result in less than 0.05 acre of fill, which would have negligible effects on
aquatic species. Vibratory and impact pile driving would not occur simultaneously and only one
pile driver would be used at any given time. Pile driving would include the use of a Micarta pile

pile driving would be used at the start of each pile to give mobile species an opportunity to vacate
the pile driving area. The jetty and MOF structures would be constructed within dredged areas
and would have no additional effects on shallow water habitat. The piles and Marine Facilities
would provide new vertical structures and shading within the water column that species could use
for shelter.

work with the USACE to design and implement an Aquatic Resources Mitigation Plan. This plan
aims to offset the loss of wetlands, including low marsh and seagrass, that would be affected by
the conversion to deepwater habitat. CCL Stage IV currently anticipates mitigating for permanent
losses of wetlands and seagrass within the watershed or an adjacent watershed at a 3:1 ratio.

Turbidity and Sedimentation

        Dredging and marine facility construction activities would result in temporary increases in
turbidity and sedimentation within EFH. Elevated turbidity can decrease habitat quality and


                                                 4-27
 modify habitat function, possibly harming fish or altering their behavior. Additionally, these
activities could affect the filtration capabilities of filter-feeding benthic organisms by causing
either clogging or complete burial. Suspended sediments may reduce water quality including
dissolved oxygen level, pH, temperature, and clarity; reduce light penetration, especially to
photosynthetic species such as seagrasses; affect feeding activity in invertebrates; scour external
surfaces of benthic organisms; and clog filtration systems or digestive organs in invertebrates, or
gills in fish entrained in the plume (Kerr, 1995; Bell et al., 2015). Settlement of suspended
sediments in areas outside of the immediate Project workspace may smother benthic organisms,
such as fish eggs, filter feeders, and seagrass. Larger plumes of sediment can affect fish
movements and cause avoidance, feeding impairment, physiological changes, altered growth rates,
reduced fecundity, and reduced quality of food sources (Kerr, 1995).

         Substrates of the La Quinta Ship Channel within the Project area consist mainly of soft
sediments, though clay, silt, and sand sediments are known to occur throughout much of Corpus
Christi Bay area. 66 CCL Stage IV would use hydraulic suction cutter dredging to reduce
sedimentation and turbidity effects from dredging. Any suspended sediments that would result
from hydraulic dredging would remain within a few hundred feet of the dredging footprint and
would settle within hours of dredging completion. The effects of turbidity and sedimentation are
anticipated to be minimal, localized, and short-term due to the following factors: substrates that
generally produce low turbidity, existing turbid conditions within the La Quinta Ship Channel,
ability to adjust the cutterhead speed to suit the sediment type, and minimal sediment dispersion
due to slow water movement within the La Qunita Ship Channel. In addition, CCL Stage IV
committed to installing turbidity curtains and/or comparable best management practices during
construction, as needed, to protect adjacent resources from turbidity and sedimentation.

        Routine maintenance dredging of the proposed marine berth pocket would occur no more
frequently than once every 10 years. These maintenance activities would produce similar, but
shorter-term, environmental effects compared to initial dredging. Therefore, effects of turbidity
and sedimentation on fisheries and aquatic resources would be moderate but not significant.

Ballast Water

        Ships berthed at the CCL Terminal would discharge ballast water while loading LNG.
Ballast water discharges can affect salinity, dissolved oxygen, water temperature, and pH of the
receiving waters if the volume of the discharges is significant enough to affect the ability of the
receiving water to absorb and circulate the discharges. Corpus Christi Bay is a hypersaline estuary
with an average salinity of 30.82 parts per thousand (as measured between the years 1987 and
2016), which is near the typical salinity of sea water (approximately 34–36 parts per thousand)
(Montagna, et al., 2021). Localized changes in salinity from ballast water are anticipated to be
minor and within the tolerable ranges of fisheries species and would be consistent in pH, dissolved
oxygen, and temperature.

         Ballast water discharge also has the potential to introduce and spread nonindigenous
species. As it pertains to invasive and nonindigenous species, the United States regulates ballast
water management domestically through the USCG under the Nonindigenous Aquatic Nuisance
Prevention and Control Act of 1990, as amended by the National Invasive Species Act of 1996 (16
United States Code [USC] §4701), and through the USEPA Vessel General Permit program, issued
under Section 402 of the CWA (33 USC §1342). All ballast water discharges would comply with
these regulations and LNGCs calling at the CCL Terminal and would either be fitted with USCG
type approved ballast water management system to meet discharge standards (USCG, 2017) or
would temporarily use an Alternate Management System for the ballast system on board (USCG,
2024a; 77 Federal Register at 17259). In addition, the International Maritime Organization
introduced global standards to reduce the risk of invasive species introductions via ballast water
through adoption of the International Convention for the Control and Management of Ships’
Ballast Water and Sediments (International Maritime Organization, 2017). LNGCs travelling
internationally would be required to adhere to these standards. With these measures in place, the
risk to fishery and aquatic resources from the introduction of non-native species into Waters of the
United States has been reduced and would not be significant.

Cooling Water

         During arrival, loading, and departure from the berths, LNGCs would draw cooling water
from the La Quinta Ship Channel to keep their main engines and auxiliary equipment cool and
within the prescribed operation temperatures. The cooling water is withdrawn and discharged
below the water line through screened intake ports on the sides of the ship. We do not expect the
temperature increase from discharged water to exceed approximately 12 degrees Celsius (°C) and
would return to ambient temperatures within about 3 feet horizontally and 25 feet vertically from
the discharge point (Tetra Tech, 2012). While elevated temperatures may pose a risk to marine
life directly within the discharge zone, the large volume of surrounding bay water would facilitate
rapid dilution and temperature normalization of the water. These thermal effects are temporary
and limited to the duration of cargo loading (estimated at 18 to 30 hours). Additionally, most
mobile aquatic species, such as fishes, are capable of avoiding the affected area, reducing the
likelihood of significant ecological effects from the cooling water discharge.

         Cooling water intake by LNGCs could also affect ichthyoplankton (very small or
sometimes microscopic fish eggs and larvae that are planktonic or “free floating”) and other small,
free floating aquatic species by impingement and entrainment. Entrainment losses can be put into
perspective through Equivalent Adult Model calculations to estimate the number of equivalent
adults that are represented by the losses of eggs and larvae (Dixon, 2007). A study in the Delaware
River Estuary using an Equivalent Adult Model to estimate the entrainment of ichthyoplankton by
LNGC ballast water intake systems projected the number of adults lost would be very small (a
maximum of 0.12 percent) and thus suggested that intake operations would have very little effect
on regional fish populations (Prakash et al., 2014). Injury and mortality of planktonic fisheries
organisms due to entrainment during cooling water intake is expected, but the percentage of
planktonic fisheries organisms affected would not be extensive enough to have a significant effect
on the fisheries and aquatic resources of the area.
